extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional theory, historians, and policymakers interested in parliamentary/constitutional government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the substantive conditions, risks, and institutional principles that make cabinet/parliamentary government work (and the limits of monarchical powers). Focuses on qualities needed in monarchs, the uses/misuses of peer-creation and dismissal powers, and the social prerequisites for elective cabinet government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in a monarch to dissolve Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: To dissolve Parliament efficiently a man must be, if not a great statesman, yet a considerable statesman. He must have great natural vigour, for no less will comprehend the hard principles of national policy. He must have incessant industry, for no less will keep him abreast with the involved detail to which those principles relate, and the miscellaneous occasions to which they must be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and anti-patterns: a monarch 'in the recesses of a palace, listening to a charmed flattery' and hedged by rank is unlikely to possess these qualities; such a life will not teach tact for public opinion and will probably enfeeble it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger when monarch appeals from wise Parliament to a sullen nation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crown can, and sometimes will, 'appeal from a wise and pacific Parliament to a sullen and warlike nation.' (Example: George III during the American war undermining Lord North and Parliament's wisest course.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences/anti-patterns: this check can be misused to curb parliamentary wisdom, prolong disastrous policies (e.g., war), and override a pacific Parliament by mobilising a less-informed nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premier and Parliament generally better placed than monarch on great occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: The preponderant probability is that on a great occasion the Premier and Parliament will really be wiser than the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: the Premier is accountable (loses office if he fails) which sharpens judgment; Parliament is 'for the most part a sound, careful, and practical body of men.' By contrast the king is exempt from such penalties and less likely to have the necessary industry or discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical royal powers have largely dropped from constitutional reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dismiss a Government or dissolve Parliament 'indisputably, in theory, belongs' to the sovereign; but in practice it has 'almost, if not quite, dropped out of the reality of our constitution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative point: although legally retained, the intervention of the Crown (e.g., destroying a ministry trusted by Parliament) would now astonish and terrify the public; historical precedents (e.g., William IV's dismissal) demonstrate political risk and unpopularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch as safety-valve vs. premier — potential value but practical rarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A good, capable, hereditary monarch would exercise certain reserve powers (the 'safety-valve') better than a premier, but a premier could manage it well enough; a monarch capable of doing better will be born only once in a century, whereas monarchs likely to do worse will be born every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off: while a wise, impartial monarch at a crisis could be 'priceless' in averting turmoil, the empirical probability of having such a monarch when needed is low, making reliance on hereditary monarchy risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of the Crown's peer-creation power: ordinary (gradual) and catastrophic (swamping)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two modes in which the power to create Peers acts: one constant, habitual (a few year by year), which continually modifies the House of Lords; and the other possible and terrific — a catastrophic creation designed to change the majority suddenly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional distinction: ordinary gradual creations harmonise the upper house with public opinion and are valuable in the premier's hands; catastrophic creations are extreme, reserved for great occasions, and have different institutional requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastrophic peer-creation is best in the hands of an able, impartial monarch
rubrics_metrics.description: If an able and impartial exterior king is at hand, this power is best in that king. It is a power only to be used on great occasions, when the object is immense and party strife unmitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: catastrophic creation is a 'conclusive' swaying power for the moment and therefore should ideally be executed by someone impartial and capable rather than by a partisan premier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical anti-patterns show danger of entrusting peer-creation to weak monarchs
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Queen Anne's capricious creations (influenced by a waiting‑maid) and William IV's vacillation over making peers during the Reform Bill crisis illustrate that weak or capricious sovereigns can misuse or mishandle this power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takeaway: these cases show uncertainty and personal idiosyncrasy can provoke crises; 'you may place power in weak hands at a revolution, but you cannot keep it in weak hands' — it will run out into stronger hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal safeguard proposal for extraordinary peer-creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rule: an extraordinary number of Peers (say, more than ten annually) should not be created except on a vote of some large majority — suppose three‑fourths of the lower house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to ensure the premier does not use the reserve force as an ordinary force, to keep it for revolutionary moments, and to ensure it is used only when the whole nation fixedly wishes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite of elective/cabinet government: mutual confidence of electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The first pre-requisite of elective government is the mutual confidence of the electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: in semi-barbarous or highly localised societies wide distrust prevents cooperation between regions; successful indirect election and representative government rely on citizens' trust in one another to choose rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite of elective government: a calm national mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A calm national mind — a tone of mind sufficiently stable to bear the necessary excitement of conspicuous revolutions — is a very rare condition of elective government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role of august institutions: symbols like a hereditary sovereign help prevent collapse by preserving reverence; poorer, less educated classes may believe the sovereign governs and so be spared the disruptive excitement of direct political action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite of elective government: rationality (ability to form distant conceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third condition (called 'rationality') is a power involving intelligence distinct from it: a whole people electing its rulers must be able to form a distinct conception of distant objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: electorate must be able to think beyond local prejudices and imagine the needs and characters of distant regions and representatives; absence of this faculty undermines representative/elective systems.
